paragraphs: This paper studies decisions made over time when their rewards and resource costs become known only after each decision. Rewards have a diminishing-returns structure called DR-submodularity. The decisions must also meet convex constraints on average, making the setting relevant to resource budgets that apply across many rounds rather than separately at every round.

The authors consider two ways constraints can change: arbitrarily, as in an adversarial setting, or through independent draws from a fixed distribution. They propose one algorithm that works in both settings without needing advance knowledge of which regime applies. This removes the need to select a different method based on how constraints arrive.

The analysis establishes regret and cumulative constraint-violation bounds that grow sublinearly with the number of rounds. Consequently, the corresponding bounds per round decrease as the horizon grows; this is not a promise of satisfying every individual constraint immediately. The results improve earlier bounds for linear constraints and extend sublinear guarantees to general convex long-term constraints.
neurips-2020-a-single-recipe-for-online-.tldr: One online optimization algorithm achieves sublinear regret and constraint violation under both adversarial and stochastic convex constraints.

paragraphs: Positive-and-unlabeled learning trains a binary classifier from confirmed positive examples and examples whose class is unknown. The unlabeled group cannot simply be treated as negative. This situation arises when verifying negatives is difficult, including the text classification, disease gene identification, and fraud detection applications discussed in the paper.

Many existing approaches adapt the misclassification-risk objective used in supervised learning. They can depend on estimating class prior probabilities, meaning the overall proportions of the classes, and inaccurate estimates can undermine learning. The paper introduces a variational principle that evaluates the modeling error of the Bayesian classifier directly from the available data.

This principle produces a loss that can be calculated efficiently without estimating class priors or solving other intermediate estimation problems. The classifier can then be optimized through variational learning under general conditions. Benchmark examples illustrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a direct training objective for the available positive and unlabeled observations, avoiding an estimation step that can otherwise introduce error.
neurips-2020-a-variational-approach-for-.tldr: A variational objective trains classifiers from positive and unlabeled data without estimating class prior probabilities.

paragraphs: Deep learning compilers search for efficient implementations of tensor computations, but finding a fast implementation can itself take a long time. AdaTune addresses this optimization cost. Its target is the process of tuning programs for inference, where repeated hardware measurements and searching among program transformations consume substantial time.

The method combines three adaptive components. A statistical evaluation procedure can stop expensive hardware measurements early while sacrificing little accuracy. A surrogate model represents uncertainty to better accommodate differences between hardware and models. A contextual optimizer adjusts the balance between exploring new transformations and exploiting promising ones, improving how the search spends its budget.

Experiments report up to 115% higher GFLOPS than the baseline compiler under equal optimization-time budgets. When matching optimization quality instead, AdaTune reduces optimization time by factors of 1.3 to 3.9 across a range of models and hardware architectures. These are complementary findings: the method can find faster programs within a fixed tuning budget or reach comparable program quality with less tuning.
neurips-2020-adatune-adaptive-tensor-pro.tldr: AdaTune makes tensor-program tuning more efficient through adaptive measurements, uncertainty-aware modeling, and contextual search.

paragraphs: Organizations can benefit from one another's information while pursuing different prediction tasks, yet restrictions on sharing data and modeling methods often prevent direct collaboration. Assisted Learning proposes a framework for supervised learning in which organizations help one another without revealing their algorithms, underlying data, or even the tasks they are trying to solve.

An organization requests assistance by broadcasting statistics that relate to its task but are described as nonsensitive. Other organizations provide feedback, which the requesting organization incorporates into its own learning process. This exchange can happen once or over several iterations. Collaboration therefore proceeds through useful statistical feedback while each participant retains its own learning setup.

Theoretical and experimental studies, including medical benchmarks, indicate that the framework can often approach the performance of an oracle with centralized data and training. The qualification matters: near-centralized performance is reported as something frequently achievable, not guaranteed for every collaboration. The findings suggest that carefully structured assistance can recover substantial predictive benefits even when pooling the original learning resources is restricted.
neurips-2020-assisted-learning-a-framewo.tldr: Assisted Learning lets organizations improve predictions through statistical feedback while keeping their data, algorithms, and tasks private.

paragraphs: Many physics and engineering simulators can produce outcomes for chosen parameters without supplying derivatives that reveal how to improve those parameters. Optimization becomes especially difficult when outputs are stochastic and their likelihoods are intractable. This paper proposes using differentiable learned models to make gradient-based optimization possible for such black-box simulators.

The method repeatedly trains deep generative models to approximate the simulator within local neighborhoods of parameter space. These local surrogates supply approximate gradients, which guide changes to the simulator's parameters. Local approximation is central to the approach: the learned model is used to describe behavior around the region currently relevant to optimization.

The authors demonstrate that the surrogate gradients can support optimization. They observe faster attainment of minima than Bayesian optimization, numerical optimization, and score-function gradient approaches in cases where simulator dependence lies on a low-dimensional submanifold. That condition is part of the reported finding. The result supports local generative approximation as a useful route when the effective parameter dependence has this structure.
neurips-2020-black-box-optimization-with.tldr: Differentiable local generative models provide approximate gradients for optimizing stochastic black-box simulators.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples to supplement a limited labeled dataset. A common mechanism assigns model-generated labels, or pseudo-labels, to unlabeled data. When training classes are imbalanced, these predictions can favor majority classes, creating problems when evaluation gives balanced importance to the classes rather than following the training imbalance.

DARP addresses this problem by refining the pseudo-labels produced by the biased model. The authors express the refinement as a convex optimization problem and develop an algorithm that solves it provably and efficiently. The adjustment is soft, allowing the label information to be refined rather than treating every original prediction as an unquestionable class assignment.

Experiments across several imbalanced semi-supervised scenarios demonstrate the method's effectiveness and compatibility with leading semi-supervised learning schemes. The contribution targets a specific source of error: the class bias carried into training through pseudo-labels. Its compatibility matters because pseudo-label refinement can improve how existing schemes use unlabeled data without requiring a wholly separate approach to semi-supervised learning.
neurips-2020-distribution-aligning-refin.tldr: DARP efficiently refines biased pseudo-labels to improve semi-supervised learning with imbalanced classes.

paragraphs: This paper develops algorithms for estimating how different two high-dimensional probability distributions are. The target quantity is total variation distance, and the algorithms approximate it within an additive error. Their sample requirements and running times are polynomial in the number of variables and the inverse of the requested error tolerance.

The results cover several structured families with specific conditions: Bayesian networks with known directed acyclic graphs and bounded in-degree, ferromagnetic Ising models with bounded width, and multivariate Gaussian distributions. Another result uses observations from causal models with known graphs to approximate the distance between distributions produced by a specified intervention on one variable.

Distance estimates also yield tolerant closeness tests, which accommodate small discrepancies rather than requiring distributions to match exactly. The authors report new tolerant testers for Bayesian networks and Ising models and quantitative testing guarantees for interventional distributions. A general framework connects these algorithms. Their significance is that useful structural information enables efficient quantitative comparison across several otherwise challenging high-dimensional settings.
neurips-2020-efficient-distance-approxim.tldr: A general framework efficiently approximates total variation distance for several structured distribution families, including specified causal interventions.

paragraphs: Generating a structured object requires more than producing something that resembles training examples. Molecules must meet chemical validity requirements, and game maps can have structural rules. The paper argues that ordinary adversarial training struggles to acquire such hard requirements from examples alone, motivating a way to incorporate explicit constraints during learning.

Constrained Adversarial Networks extend GANs by penalizing the generator according to the probability mass it places on invalid structures. They support arbitrary logical constraints and use knowledge compilation to evaluate disagreement with those constraints efficiently. The framework also includes hybrid logical-neural constraints for more complex properties, such as whether locations in a graph are reachable.

The authors report efficient generation of valid structures with high probability, together with empirical evidence of quality and novelty. High probability is the stated validity claim, rather than certainty for every generated object. The method also allows learned constraints to be switched on or off during inference, providing control over which requirements apply when producing outputs.
neurips-2020-efficient-generation-of-str.tldr: Constrained Adversarial Networks train generators with explicit logical requirements to efficiently produce valid structures with high probability.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can deteriorate when compromised workers send malicious information. This paper focuses on SignSGD, where workers communicate gradient signs to a master. Election Coding applies coding theory to protect this communication-efficient learning setup, studying how the master can recover the correct majority opinion despite adversarial interference from workers.

The framework introduces random Bernoulli codes and deterministic algebraic codes. Both use controlled computational redundancy to tolerate Byzantine attacks, and the authors establish convergence guarantees in general nonconvex scenarios. For the random codes, an upper bound on the probability of incorrectly estimating true gradient signs helps connect code design to robustness.

For the deterministic construction, the authors prove perfect tolerance of arbitrary Byzantine attacks within the coding framework. This is a guarantee tied to the proposed construction and its redundancy, rather than a statement about unprotected distributed systems. Experiments on real datasets show substantial improvements in attack tolerance for SignSGD. The work connects reliable aggregation, communication efficiency, and extra computation in a single design.
neurips-2020-election-coding-for-distrib.tldr: Election Coding uses computational redundancy and coding theory to make communication-efficient SignSGD robust to Byzantine attacks.

paragraphs: Entropic causal inference seeks the causal direction between two categorical variables using observational data. Its central assumption limits the amount of hidden randomness driving their relationship. The framework measures that randomness through the entropy of an exogenous variable in a structural causal model, making a restriction on unseen variation central to identifying direction.

The paper proves a variant of an earlier conjecture: direction is identifiable for almost all causal models whose exogenous entropy does not grow with the number of observed-variable states. The authors also provide finite-sample algorithmic identifiability guarantees for an approach based on minimum entropy coupling, connecting the structural result to inference from a limited dataset.

Experiments investigate robustness when theoretical assumptions are relaxed. They indicate that constant exogenous entropy and the absence of latent confounders can be relaxed in practice, without making those relaxations part of the general theorem. The authors also examine sample requirements empirically and apply the algorithm to Tuebingen cause-effect pairs. The work separates formal identifiability conditions from evidence of broader practical usefulness.
neurips-2020-entropic-causal-inference-i.tldr: The paper establishes causal-direction identifiability under bounded hidden entropy and gives finite-sample guarantees for an entropy-based inference method.

paragraphs: Image-based 3D shape retrieval searches a database of shapes for a match to a two-dimensional image. A common approach places images and shapes in a shared representation space and learns their similarity. Fine-grained retrieval remains difficult because small geometric differences must be distinguished across these different forms of visual input.

The paper identifies an obstacle in metric learning: differences in shape become entangled with differences in texture. This can make learning to separate nonmatching pairs ineffective. The proposed framework synthesizes textures for 3D models to create difficult training triplets and combines them with geometry-focused, multi-view metric learning.

These examples suppress the distracting influence of rich image textures and encourage the network to discover geometric characteristics. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on 3D-FUTURE, Pix3D, Stanford Cars, and Comp Cars. The finding supports deliberately shaping training difficulty around the desired similarity criterion: here, the training examples push the learned representation toward geometry when appearance differences would otherwise interfere.
neurips-2020-hard-example-generation-by-.tldr: Synthesized textures create difficult training examples that help image-to-3D retrieval models focus on geometry.

paragraphs: An autoencoder maps inputs into latent codes and reconstructs them through a decoder. Controlling the information capacity of those codes is an important design choice. This paper focuses on their effective dimension: a representation can contain many coordinates while its variation across examples occupies a much smaller set of directions.

The proposed Implicit Rank-Minimizing Autoencoder inserts several additional linear layers between encoder and decoder. It relies on the tendency of gradient descent in multilayer linear networks to produce minimum-rank solutions. Through this training behavior, the model implicitly minimizes the rank of the codes' covariance matrix and learns representations with low effective dimension.

IRMAE is described as simple and deterministic, with a continuous latent space. The authors demonstrate the method on several image generation and representation learning tasks. The central contribution is a way to limit latent capacity through the interaction between architecture and optimization. Extra linear layers serve as the mechanism encouraging low-dimensional codes, rather than making latent width alone the measure of capacity.
neurips-2020-implicit-rank-minimizing-au.tldr: IRMAE adds linear layers between encoder and decoder so gradient-based training implicitly encourages low-dimensional latent representations.

paragraphs: Prototype-driven text generation first retrieves an example sentence and then modifies it to produce new text. Keeping and indexing the entire training corpus makes this approach expensive at generation time. Existing methods can also rely on hand-designed rules to decide which examples should act as prototypes during training.

The proposed generative model learns a small support set of prototypes automatically. A sparsity-inducing prior encourages the selection distribution to concentrate on fewer examples, while amortized variational inference learns the retrieval function. Together, these components address both the size of the stored prototype library and the way prototypes are selected.

Experiments show better language modeling performance than earlier prototype-driven models, alongside memory reductions and test-time speedups reaching 1,000-fold. Changing the degree of sparsity also changes the granularity of semantic and syntactic information captured by the prototypes. Specifying a prototype can control certain sentence attributes. Thus, the learned library offers both computational savings and a handle on some properties of generated text.
neurips-2020-learning-sparse-prototypes-.tldr: A learned sparse prototype library improves prototype-based language modeling while sharply reducing storage and generation costs.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning several linear classifiers from binary responses when the classifier answering each query is chosen randomly. Each query is a vector, and the response indicates which side of one unknown hyperplane it occupies. The objective is to recover the entire collection, even though individual responses do not identify which classifier produced them.

The authors focus on sparse classifiers, represented by vectors with few nonzero entries. With one unknown vector, the setting becomes the extreme quantization problem known as one-bit compressed sensing. Multiple unknown vectors add uncertainty about the source of each answer, while receiving only a sign removes the numerical information available in an analogous regression problem.

The contribution consists of rigorous query-complexity results together with efficient recovery algorithms. These results address how many queries are sufficient to recover the unknown collection in the studied setting. Their importance is in establishing algorithmic guarantees for learning heterogeneous categorical behavior from highly compressed, mixed responses, extending beyond the single-classifier case.
neurips-2020-recovery-of-sparse-linear-c.tldr: The paper gives efficient algorithms and query-complexity guarantees for recovering sparse linear classifiers from randomly mixed binary responses.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether adversarially robust prediction can be learned using only an ordinary learning algorithm as a black box. The setting is standard PAC learning, where a learner is available for a hypothesis class. The challenge is to use that capability to learn predictors that remain reliable under the allowed adversarial changes to examples.

The authors give a reduction that robustly learns any hypothesis class using any non-robust learner for that class. A reduction supplies a way to solve one learning problem through calls to a solver for another. Here, access to the ordinary learner is the resource being measured, rather than access to its internal implementation.

The number of learner calls depends logarithmically on how many perturbations are allowed per example. The paper also proves a lower bound showing that this dependence cannot be avoided in the studied problem. Together, the construction and lower bound characterize an essential cost of turning ordinary learning access into robust learning capability.
neurips-2020-reducing-adversarially-robu.tldr: Robust learning can be reduced to black-box ordinary PAC learning with an unavoidable logarithmic dependence on the number of allowed perturbations.

paragraphs: Multi-task reinforcement learning aims to learn behavior for many tasks at once. Experience collected for one task may also be useful for another if it is assigned a different reward function. Earlier relabeling methods exploit this reuse, improving how much learning can be extracted from interactions that have already occurred.

The paper connects hindsight relabeling to inverse reinforcement learning. If an observed experience is treated as optimal for some task, inverse RL asks which task could explain it. The authors use this connection as a principled mechanism for assigning past experience to other tasks, extending goal-relabeling techniques to arbitrary types of reward functions.

Experiments show that inverse-RL relabeling outperforms earlier relabeling methods on goal-reaching tasks. It also accelerates learning in broader multi-task settings where those methods do not apply, including discrete sets of rewards and linear reward functions. The findings support using inferred task explanations to reuse experience beyond settings defined only by reaching a different goal.
neurips-2020-rewriting-history-with-inve.tldr: Inverse reinforcement learning provides a principled way to relabel past experience for reuse across tasks with diverse reward functions.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks learn from data whose relationships form a graph, but handling billions of edges creates substantial computational challenges. Sampling graphs or individual layers can reduce training work, yet the paper describes continuing problems with scalability and predictive performance. GBP is designed to make learning practical on graphs at this scale.

Its central mechanism is localized bidirectional propagation, proceeding from both the feature vector and the nodes used for training or testing. The theoretical analysis establishes sublinear time complexity for both precomputation and training. The authors identify this combination of guarantees as a first, addressing preparation costs as well as the subsequent learning phase.

Empirical evaluations report state-of-the-art performance with substantially reduced training and testing time. In the largest highlighted example, GBP delivers superior performance on a graph containing more than 60 million nodes and 1.8 billion edges in under 2,000 seconds on one machine. This demonstrates the practical scale reached by the method alongside its theoretical efficiency results.
neurips-2020-scalable-graph-neural-netwo.tldr: GBP uses localized bidirectional propagation to make graph neural network precomputation and training scalable to billion-edge graphs.

paragraphs: A neural ordinary differential equation model computes its forward pass by solving an ODE. As training changes the learned dynamics, solving that equation can become increasingly complex and expensive. Earlier work has addressed part of this cost by regularizing the dynamics, encouraging behavior that is easier to handle during computation.

STEER introduces a simple temporal regularizer: randomly sample the ODE's end time during training. This changes the duration over which the model evolves while it learns. The authors describe the procedure as easy to implement with negligible overhead. It is also compatible with several other dynamics regularizers, allowing the approaches to be used together.

Experiments span normalizing flows, time-series models, and image recognition. They show that the method can substantially reduce training time and can also improve performance over baseline models. These are empirical benefits across the tested tasks, rather than a universal speed guarantee. The contribution makes the integration endpoint itself a useful and inexpensive part of regularization.
neurips-2020-steer-simple-temporal-regul.tldr: STEER randomly varies the integration end time during neural ODE training, reducing training cost and sometimes improving predictive performance.

paragraphs: Sequential predictions often need to obey known properties, such as reasonable value ranges, resource restrictions, or temporal relationships between variables. A recurrent neural network trained from data alone does not guarantee that its predictions will satisfy these requirements. Violations can make predictions inaccurate or meaningless, particularly in complex cyber-physical systems.

STLnet introduces a temporal-logic learning framework that uses knowledge of these properties to guide training. It incorporates requirements about how sequences should behave into the learning process. The framework supports general sequential deep learning models and can be trained end to end with backpropagation, connecting explicit model knowledge with standard neural training.

Evaluation on large-scale real-world city data reports improved prediction accuracy and robustness, together with guaranteed satisfaction of model properties. The relevant properties are those supplied to the framework, which gives the satisfaction claim a concrete target. The results show the value of evaluating sequence predictions by whether they follow known system requirements as well as whether they match observed values.
neurips-2020-stlnet-signal-temporal-logi.tldr: STLnet uses temporal logic to guide sequential neural models toward accurate, robust predictions that satisfy specified model properties.

paragraphs: Channel pruning reduces the channels used by a convolutional neural network. Runtime pruning can adapt those choices to each input, but the paper identifies a storage problem: existing runtime methods still require all channel parameters to be stored for inference. Dynamic computation therefore does not automatically provide a corresponding reduction in parameter storage.

The proposed framework uses deep reinforcement learning to learn a pruning strategy. For each input, the strategy decides both how many channels to prune and which channels to remove in each convolutional layer. A static pruning component reduces the parameters that must be stored, while runtime decisions retain input-dependent flexibility.

Experiments compare the framework with existing runtime and static pruning methods on state-of-the-art convolutional networks. The results demonstrate a tradeoff between dynamic flexibility and storage efficiency. The contribution is the combination of these two pruning roles: permanent pruning addresses storage consumption, while learned runtime choices adapt the remaining computation to individual inputs.
neurips-2020-storage-efficient-and-dynam.tldr: A reinforcement-learning pruning framework combines input-dependent channel selection with static pruning to balance flexibility and parameter storage.

paragraphs: Feature distillation transfers information from a teacher network's internal features to a student network. Many existing methods use a manually designed transformation to prepare the teacher features for this transfer. This paper asks how that transformation can instead be learned so that the transferred information is oriented toward the prediction task.

Task-oriented feature distillation uses convolutional layers as the transformation and trains them through the task loss. This makes the transformation data-driven and allows task-relevant feature information to be captured for the student. The method also applies an orthogonal loss to its feature-resizing layer as an additional component intended to improve distillation performance.

Experiments on image classification and 3D classification show TOFD outperforming other distillation methods by a large margin. These findings support learning how features are transformed as part of the task itself. The contribution places the transformation inside the optimization process, giving the task objective a direct role in determining what information is passed from teacher to student.
neurips-2020-task-oriented-feature-disti.tldr: TOFD learns feature transformations through task loss to transfer task-relevant information from teacher networks to students.

paragraphs: SLOPE generalizes the lasso for selecting relevant predictors, particularly when predictors greatly outnumber observations. Its numerical procedures have lacked some of the efficiency available for the lasso, especially when fitting models across a regularization path. Screening rules offer one route to faster fitting by discarding predictors before solving each model.

The authors derive a screening rule from SLOPE's subdifferential, the mathematical object describing its generalized slopes. Their rule extends the lasso's strong screening rule to SLOPE. It is heuristic and can wrongly discard useful predictors, so the paper includes a safeguard based on checking optimality conditions. The authors report that such errors are rare.

Numerical experiments show improvements by orders of magnitude when predictors greatly outnumber observations, with no additional computational overhead when observations outnumber predictors. The safeguard is important to interpreting the method: the speedup comes from aggressive screening paired with a check, rather than an assertion that screening never makes mistakes. This makes a key computational strategy available for SLOPE fitting.
neurips-2020-the-strong-screening-rule-f.tldr: A heuristic screening rule accelerates SLOPE fitting, with optimality checks guarding against incorrectly discarded predictors.

paragraphs: A GAN generator learns from feedback supplied by a critic about generated samples. This paper changes which samples contribute when the generator is updated. Instead of using every element of a batch, it sets the gradient contributions of the critic's least-realistic samples to zero, leaving the better-scoring samples to drive the update.

The modification is described as one line of code with no increase in computational cost. Experiments across many GAN variants support its broad applicability. To investigate why it helps, the authors analyze a mixture-of-Gaussians dataset and find that updates based on the worst-scoring samples can move samples farther from their nearest mode.

That observation shows why strongly criticized samples need not always provide useful generator updates. The authors also apply top-k training to leading GAN models, including BigGAN. For conditional CIFAR-10 generation, they improve the reported state-of-the-art FID from 9.21 to 8.57. The results support selectively using critic feedback as a simple way to improve GAN training.
neurips-2020-top-k-training-of-gans-impr.tldr: Updating GAN generators using only better-scoring batch samples improves results without increasing computational cost.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates how a policy performs from experience. In the off-policy setting, that experience can come from a different policy. This paper develops variance reduction for TDC, a temporal-difference method with two time scales, and studies convergence after a finite number of samples rather than only eventual limiting behavior.

The analysis covers both independent samples and Markovian samples, which capture sequential dependence. With independent samples, the reported sample-complexity bound improves from order epsilon to the minus one times log of inverse epsilon to order epsilon to the minus three-fifths times that logarithm. Here epsilon represents the target error tolerance.

For Markovian samples, the method achieves the state-of-the-art bound of order inverse epsilon times log of inverse epsilon, described as near-optimal. Experiments also show smaller asymptotic convergence error than conventional TDC and variance-reduced TD. The distinction between sampling regimes matters: the improved independent-sample rate and the near-optimal sequential-sample rate are separate results for the same proposed scheme.
neurips-2020-variance-reduced-off-policy.tldr: Variance-reduced off-policy TDC improves independent-sample complexity and achieves a near-optimal bound for Markovian samples.

paragraphs: Wide neural networks can behave like kernel methods under one scaling of initialization, yet neural networks can outperform them under another. This paper investigates how these observations fit together. It focuses on the relationship between the structure of the input variables and the low-dimensional structure of the function being learned.

When inputs are nearly isotropic, kernel methods face a curse of dimensionality, while neural networks can learn a useful low-dimensional representation. The authors show that this disadvantage becomes milder when the input distribution already shares the target function's low-dimensional structure. They characterize the tradeoff and introduce a spiked covariates model that captures both patterns within one framework.

The authors hypothesize that a similar latent structure exists in image classification. Numerical tests show that specific perturbations of the training distribution hurt kernel methods much more than neural networks. These experiments support the hypothesis without establishing it universally. The work explains why comparing the methods requires attention to input geometry as well as the target function.
neurips-2020-when-do-neural-networks-out.tldr: The advantage of neural networks over kernel methods depends partly on whether inputs already share the target function's low-dimensional structure.
